content_summary.overview: A history-of-thought paper. Leslie (1825-82), Irish political economist, TCD gold medallist 1847, LLB 1851, professor of jurisprudence and political economy at Queen's College Belfast 1853-82. Argues that the Irish land question drove Leslie's critique of Ricardian rent theory and the 'classical landed property reform' (consolidation into large capitalist farms on the English tripartite landlord/capitalist-tenant/labourer model), and that Leslie, a self-proclaimed Millian, pushed beyond Mill by recommending small proprietorships for England as well as Ireland. Sections: II enclosure, urbanisation and necessity of land reform (pp.5-7); III Land Systems (1870) as historical-institutionalist critique (pp.7-11); IV the 'double rejection of classical and Fenian solutions' (pp.11-14); V small proprietorship and the state, birth of Irish historical economics (pp.14-20).
key_points: Method: inductive, historical-comparative, institutionalist; law, history, geography; 'relativity of economic doctrines'; influenced by Smith, Mill, Maine (status to contract) and de Laveleye (small-farming surveys), de Lavergne (pp.4, 8, 11, 17).

Enclosure: reads the 18th-19th C enclosures as a restoration of 'feudal' property rights and 'confiscation' of the peasantry's patrimony; compares with Marx's primitive accumulation (Manioudis's gloss, p.5); commons loss, farm consolidation and rent rises (pp.5-6).

Urbanisation: forced rural-urban migration, rising house rents, overcrowding, in 'seven large towns' (5,153,157 persons, early 1870s per Leslie 1870c p.205) (p.6); 'status to contract' unfinished in land law, land law 'the radical cause' of pauperism (p.7).

Irish land: security of tenure as the 'law which has no exceptions' (p.10); short leases, absenteeism (pp.10); Irish rents are 'the surplus above minimum wages, without any profit at all', not the classical rent surplus (p.14); landlords as 'consumers' (p.14, fn 25).

Double rejection: against Lowe/Ricardian laissez-faire consolidation AND against Fenian separation (Leslie 1868a, 'Ireland in 1868', supplementing Mill's England and Ireland); unionist: small proprietorship as a means of defending the Act of Union (pp.11-14).

Remedy: long leases, abolition of primogeniture and entail, simple land registration, legal compensation for improvements, sale of absentee lands to tenants, a few millions of Treasury advances for tenant purchase; by 1880 state purchase of landlords' farms, with optional commutation of rents into land annuities; compensation of existing proprietors accepted (pp.14-16, 19).
1870 Act criticised for not 'boldly creating a great number of small proprietors with full ownership' (p.16); disappointment with Gladstone; no land publications 1870-80 (p.2).
Rural-urban 'natural course of things' (Smith): towns should follow the country; Irish and English agriculture made 'unnatural' by large farms (pp.7, 10-11).
Leslie remained a free-trade liberal; not a socialist or nationaliser (p.20).

from_newton_1971_supplementary.source: Bernard Newton, AJES 30:2 (April 1971), p.183, file newton-1971-manual-transcription-pp182-183.txt (hand transcription; verify against the scan PDF pp.4-5)
points: George sent Leslie a promised copy of Progress and Poverty after its publication in November 1879; Leslie replied on 26 November 1879 that although both opposed the 'School of Economics' (the English classical school) he differed from George on some points (Newton fn 14, Henry George Collection, NYPL).

In September 1880 Leslie wrote again that he had written 'Political Economy in the United States', discussing Progress and Poverty at some length, while he 'by no means sought to disparage the ability shown' (fn 15).

Newton calls it the first review of Progress and Poverty by an English academic economist (Fortnightly Review 34, 1 Oct 1880, reprinted in Leslie's Essays in Political Economy, 2nd ed. 1888, pp.147-152).

Newton's summary of Leslie's objections: Leslie, like George, rejected the wages-fund theory but could not accept George's substitute that wages are drawn from the current product of labour; Leslie argued from historical evidence that long-run wages, interest and rents had all risen in the British Isles, so George's central distribution claims were wrong.
from_newton_1971_supplementary.implication: Leslie did engage George (1879-80) and rejected key parts of Progress and Poverty's distribution theory. This is a Newton-sourced fact (Tier 1 academic, but 1971 secondary on a primary letter/essay), not a Manioudis one. The primary, Leslie's Fortnightly Review essay 'Political Economy in the United States' (1 Oct 1880; Essays in Political Economy 1888, pp.147-152), is public domain and should be fetched by T1 before the people page states Leslie's objections in his own words (archive.org / Wikisource).

Page locators are JHET (journal) pagination; the flat file marks each page [[JHET p.N]]. The first page of the PDF is p.1 (title page with abstract and Intro start).

Almost all Leslie quotations are secondary: Leslie as quoted by Manioudis, with Manioudis's page cites to Leslie's essays (1866 'Political Economy and the Tenure of Land', Fortnightly Review, reprinted in Land Systems pp.117-132; 1867a 'The State of Ireland, 1867', Macmillan's; 1868a 'Ireland in 1868', Fortnightly; 1868b 'Political Economy and Emigration', Fraser's; 1870a Land Systems; 1870b 'The Irish Land Question, 1870'; 1870c 'The English Land Question'; [1880] 1881 'The Irish Land Question', Fraser's). Exact venues in the bibliography, pp.21-23 (flat file: grep -F 'Political Economy and the Tenure of Land'). T1 should not present them as verified against the primaries; Land Systems (1870) is public domain and could be fetched for the people page.
Manioudis's year for the 1880 Frazer's Magazine essay is given as 1880 in the body and '1880s paper' in the conclusion (p.20), an apparent slip; page should say 1880.

Collison Black (2002) is cited as the source for the 'revolutionary solution' adopted by 1867 and for the commutation-into-annuities plan; Manioudis gives no independent primary page for the 1867 turn.

Leslie's seven-million-acre enclosure figure and 'small farms twice as productive' (p.17, fn 30) are Victorian claims; do not state them as fact on any wiki page. Leslie's historical claim that landholders in 1867 were fewer than at the Conquest (p.5) likewise attribute only.

Manioudis does not cover Leslie's LTRA membership; the wiki's only support is Newton 1971 p.182 (itself citing Geiger 1931 p.232n, per the scan: footnote 12 'Ibid., p. 232n', i.e. Geiger, The Philosophy of Henry George). Treat membership as single-sourced and second-hand; the LTRA's own roster (Mill's Collected Works headnote or the 1871 Programme page on the wiki) should be checked before stating it on the new people page.

Newton scan has no text layer; T0 transcribed the quoted sentences by eye. Re-check by eye. The Newton phrase that Leslie's article was 'the first review of Progress and Poverty by an English academic economist' is Newton's characterisation.
